strategy:
1. Approach and rationale
Use exact pairwise mass-exchange line searches on the discrete construction. For each pair of coordinates, hold all others fixed and transfer mass between the pair with one scalar parameter. Along that line, only three of the finite-lag overlap terms are quadratic; all others are affine. Construct the upper envelope of the affine terms, enumerate its breakpoints and the intersections and stationary points involving the three quadratics, and select the best feasible point on the line. Apply these searches in bounded pair sweeps from several deterministic feasible starts, accepting an update only when the exact evaluator score decreases.

This is materially different from both a log-sum-exp continuation with SLSQP epigraph polishing and an active-gradient method with annealed perturbations: it uses neither a smoothed objective nor a multivariate solver or gradient bundle. It exploits the special structure of two-coordinate exchanges to solve each one-dimensional restriction globally in exact arithmetic. The formulas for the lag terms and their line restrictions are exact. Multiple starts and repeated coordinate sweeps are search heuristics that may improve the supplied construction, but coordinate-wise minima can be nonglobal and no target score or global optimum is guaranteed.

2. Mathematical specification
For runtime length n, use indices i=0,...,n−1, dx=2/n, and required mass S=n/2. The feasible set is 0≤h[i]≤1 and sum_i h[i]=S. Do not change the parent resolution. The authoritative objective is C(h)=max(np.correlate(h,1−h,mode='full')*dx), including all 2n−1 finite-support lags and both directions.

For the line-search calculations, store M=2n−1 terms in this order: q[0]=dx*sum_i h[i](1−h[i]); then, for each shift d=1,...,n−1, q[2d−1]=q[d,+]=dx*sum_{i=0}^{n−d−1} h[i+d](1−h[i]) and q[2d]=q[d,−]=dx*sum_{i=0}^{n−d−1} h[i](1−h[i+d]). These shortened sums account for the partial overlap at the boundaries. Mathematically max(q)=C(h); never replace these terms with circular correlation or a full-mass identity.

For an analytic derivative matrix G of shape (M,n), set G[0,j]=dx*(1−2h[j]). For each d>0 and i=0,...,n−d−1, the plus term adds dx*(1−h[i]) to G[2d−1,i+d] and −dx*h[i+d] to G[2d−1,i]. The minus term adds dx*(1−h[i+d]) to G[2d,i] and −dx*h[i] to G[2d,i+d]. Contributions to a component from different i values must accumulate. These formulas provide the exact first derivative of each q term.

For a pair i<j, let s=j−i and h(t)=h+t(e_i−e_j). The exact feasible interval is lo=max(−h[i],h[j]−1) and hi=min(1−h[i],h[j]); it contains t=0. Each lag has the form q[l](t)=a[l]*t^2+b[l]*t+c[l], with c=q(h) and b=G[:,i]−G[:,j]. The curvature vector is sparse and known exactly: a[0]=−2dx; a[2s−1]=a[2s]=dx; all other a[l]=0. The zero-lag coefficient follows from the two changing squares in q[0]. The two shift-s terms contain the product of the changing endpoints, whose coefficient is +dx; no other nonzero-shift term contains both endpoints. Thus exactly three terms are quadratic and all remaining terms are lines in t.

Let L(t) be the maximum of the affine terms. Build its upper envelope on [lo,hi] by sorting lines by increasing slope and retaining, for equal slopes, the line with the largest intercept. In this order, the crossing of an old line (m_old,c_old) with a new line (m_new,c_new) is x=(c_old−c_new)/(m_new−m_old); pop the old hull line while x is no greater than its start point, then add the new line with start x. Clip each resulting hull segment to [lo,hi]. On each segment the full objective is the maximum of one affine line and the three quadratics. Its active branch can change only at a hull breakpoint, a quadratic-line root, or a quadratic-quadratic root. A minimum within a region with a fixed active branch is at a region endpoint unless the active branch is a convex quadratic, in which case its vertex t=−b/(2a) is also a candidate. Therefore the global minimizer of the one-dimensional maximum is among: lo and hi; affine-hull breakpoints; roots of each of the three quadratics against each affine-envelope segment; roots between each pair of the three quadratics; and vertices of positive-curvature quadratics that lie in [lo,hi]. Include t=0 as a numerical fallback candidate. Score the final vectors with the exact np.correlate evaluator, not only the polynomial values.

3. Implementation procedure
1. Define run(seed=42, **kwargs) and every helper as a top-level function. Use NumPy and math; no nested helper functions, closures, or lambdas are needed. Do not use filesystem or network I/O. The program must implement all construction, search, scoring, and fallback operations for the harness to execute.

2. Read the optional runtime global initial_h_values without redefining, serializing, hard-coding, or mutating it. Convert it to a float64 array inside exception handling. If it is one-dimensional with length at least two, its length defines n and takes precedence over kwargs n_points, even if some entries are nonfinite. A nonfinite parent is not a candidate. If no parent has a usable shape, accept kwargs n_points only when it is an integer-valued non-boolean in [2,512]; otherwise use n=42. Never resample or interpolate a usable parent. Convert seed to an integer for np.random.default_rng; if conversion fails, use 42.

3. Implement a top-level exact-score helper. For a finite vector h of length n, compute dx=2.0/n, corr=np.correlate(h,1.0−h,mode='full'), and return float(max(corr*dx)). Reject a nonfinite result. This is the sole score for candidate acceptance, incumbent comparisons, and c5_bound. Implement a separate lag helper returning q with shape (2n−1,) and G with shape (2n−1,n), using the definitions in section 2 and float64 arithmetic. Initialize G to zeros and use accumulating slice updates for every contribution. Reject nonfinite inputs or outputs.

4. Implement a feasibility predicate requiring a one-dimensional length-n finite array, every coordinate exactly within [0,1], and both abs(np.sum(h)−S) and abs(math.fsum(float(x) for x in h)−S) no greater than 1e−10. Implement a joint capped-simplex restoration helper for finite v. To avoid overflow, first clip v to [−1e6,1e6]. Find lambda by 80 bisection steps on [min(v)−1,max(v)]: form h=clip(v−lambda,0,1); if its sum exceeds S, raise the lower endpoint to the midpoint, otherwise lower the upper endpoint to the midpoint. The bracket endpoints produce all ones and all zeros respectively. After bisection, correct residual mass using math.fsum by adding only into available 1−h capacity or removing only from available h capacity, never crossing a box bound. Then try setting a coordinate with sufficient slack to S minus the stable sum of the other coordinates. Check both NumPy and stable sums and exact bounds. Return failure if the result does not meet the feasibility predicate; callers must then retain a valid candidate or use the constant fallback. Do not clip and rescale in succession.

5. Establish fallbacks before search. Construct constant_h=np.full(n,0.5), which is feasible, and compute its exact score. If the parent is finite and already satisfies the box and has mass error at most 1e−12 under both sums, retain it unchanged as the parent-derived fallback and first start. Otherwise restore it with the joint capped-simplex helper; if restoration succeeds, retain and score that repaired parent as the parent-derived fallback. Keep this fallback separately throughout the program. Initialize the global incumbent from the valid parent when present, otherwise from constant_h; compare constant_h by exact score and replace the incumbent only for an improvement greater than 1e−12.

6. Build starts using the seeded generator and a top-level add-unique helper. The helper accepts only feasible vectors and rejects a start if its maximum absolute coordinate difference from an earlier start is below 1e−10. Construct a block vector algorithmically with floor(n/2) leading ones, zeros after them, and a 0.5 at the next coordinate when n is odd. Construct an alternating 0/1 vector from index parity and project it. Construct a sinusoid as 0.5+0.45*sin(2*pi*i/n) for i=0,...,n−1 and project it. Include the constant and feasible block vectors. With a valid parent and n≤48, use starts in this order: parent, constant, block, alternating, sinusoid, two projected parent perturbations with standard deviations 0.12 and 0.35, and one projected uniform [0,1] vector. Without a valid parent and n≤48, use constant, block, alternating, sinusoid, and four independent projected uniform vectors. For 49≤n≤128, use at most the first four applicable deterministic starts: with a parent, parent, constant, block, alternating; without one, constant, block, alternating, sinusoid. Project every generated pattern, perturbation, and random vector; preserve an already feasible parent directly. Deduplicate all starts.

7. Implement the pair line search as a top-level helper taking a feasible h, i, j, and current exact score. Obtain q and G, form a, b, and c as in section 2, and compute lo and hi. Partition the lag indices into the three curved terms and the affine terms. Build the affine upper hull on [lo,hi]. Add lo, hi, and zero to a candidate-t list, along with all hull transition points. For each curved term and each affine hull segment, solve a*t^2+(b−m)*t+(c−c_line)=0 and retain roots in that segment; also solve every pairwise difference between curved terms and retain roots in [lo,hi]. Add −b/(2a) for each positive-curvature term when it lies in [lo,hi]. Sort and deduplicate candidate t values within 1e−12.

8. Implement a top-level real-root helper for A*t^2+B*t+C=0. Use tol=1e−14*max(1,abs(A),abs(B),abs(C)); when abs(A)≤tol, solve the linear equation only if abs(B)>tol. Otherwise compute the discriminant, reject it if it is less than −64*machine_epsilon*(B^2+abs(4*A*C)+1), and clamp a smaller negative discriminant to zero. Use the stable quadratic formula z=−0.5*(B+copysign(sqrt(discriminant),B)); if z is nonzero, form roots z/A and C/z, otherwise use −B/(2*A). Keep finite roots within the requested interval with a 1e−10 endpoint allowance and clamp them to the interval. When constructing the affine hull, merge slopes within 1e−14*max(1,abs(m1),abs(m2)) and keep the largest intercept. Use NumPy lexsort by slope and descending intercept rather than a lambda-based sort. If a coefficient, crossing, or hull result is nonfinite, abandon that pair update and retain h.

9. Evaluate the polynomial maximum at every candidate t using vectorized arrays: q_candidate[l]=a[l]*t^2+b[l]*t+c[l]. Sort candidates by this predicted maximum and exact-score the best six distinct t values (or all if fewer). Also retain the current vector as the baseline. Construct each trial by preserving pair_sum=h[i]+h[j]: set the new i coordinate to h[i]+t clamped to [max(0,pair_sum−1),min(1,pair_sum)], and set the new j coordinate to pair_sum minus the new i coordinate. Leave all other coordinates unchanged. Check feasibility; if roundoff makes it fail, try the joint capped-simplex restoration and score the restored vector, otherwise reject it. Exact-score every retained trial with np.correlate. Return the best feasible trial only if its exact score is lower than the current score by more than 1e−12; otherwise return the original h. The finite candidate set gives the global line minimum in exact arithmetic, while exact scoring and the improvement threshold guard against floating-point discrepancies.

10. Construct the pair schedule deterministically. For n≤48, include every unordered pair i<j. For 49≤n≤64, include canonicalized, deduplicated pairs (i,(i+r) mod n) for r in {1,2,max(1,floor(n/4)),max(1,floor(n/2))}. For 65≤n≤128, use r in {1,max(1,floor(n/2))}. Sort the deduplicated pair list, then use rng.permutation to vary its order on each sweep. For each start, initialize its current vector and exact score, visit each scheduled pair in order, and replace the current vector only when the pair helper returns an exact-score improvement. Run at most two sweeps for n≤64 and one for 65≤n≤128; stop that start early after a sweep with no accepted update. The score is monotonically decreasing within a start, so no annealed or worsening moves are used. Skip pair search entirely for n>128.

11. Process starts sequentially. After each local search, verify its length, finiteness, box, mass, and exact score before comparing it to the global incumbent. Update the incumbent only for an exact-score decrease greater than 1e−12. Catch exceptions in start construction, root calculation, or local search without losing the already validated fallbacks. For n>128, do not run the quadratic search; still score the parent-derived fallback when valid, constant_h, and the algorithmic block vector, retaining the best exact-scored feasible candidate. This preserves the parent resolution while keeping search cost bounded for larger inputs.

12. Before returning, select the lowest exact-score member of the incumbent, the separate parent fallback when present, and constant_h, using the same 1e−12 tie rule. Validate the selected vector again. If necessary, restore it jointly with the capped-simplex helper and recompute its exact score. If validation or scoring fails, return the valid parent fallback if available, otherwise constant_h, and compute that fallback's exact score. Return exactly (h_values, c5_bound, n_points), with h_values a float64 NumPy array of length n, c5_bound a Python float from the exact score helper, and n_points=int(n).

4. Search choices and useful variations
Use the defaults in section 3 without preliminary tuning: parent length fixes n; otherwise use requested integer n_points in [2,512] or default 42. Search through n=128, with eight deduplicated starts at most for n≤48, at most four starts for larger searched dimensions, the specified pair schedules, two sweeps through n=64, and one sweep above that. The supplied n=42 parent therefore receives the full pair schedule and the smaller-dimensional multistart search. All solver-like line searches and root calculations run sequentially on the single CPU.

Correctness requirements are the exact full np.correlate score, both lag orientations and finite boundaries, joint box-and-mass feasibility, exact-score candidate acceptance, unchanged parent resolution, and a separately retained validated parent fallback. Static search heuristics may vary modestly: parent perturbation scales from 0.05 to 0.4, four to ten starts, one to three sweeps for n≤48, and four to ten top polynomial candidates for exact re-scoring. Keep the stated defaults as the no-experiment choice. Any result-dependent stopping is limited to the explicit no-improvement sweep rule; do not require measurement or external tuning.

5. Numerical robustness and memory use
For n=42, q has 83 entries and G has 83*42 float64 entries, about 28 kB. The affine hull and candidate arrays are transient; the candidate-by-lag evaluation is O(n^2) storage because the number of envelope segments and roots is O(n). At n=128, G has 255*128 entries, about 255 kB, and the temporary candidate matrix remains a few megabytes. Do not form a dense Hessian, a three-dimensional lag tensor, a circular correlation, or a higher-resolution grid. The exact full correlation has length 2n−1. Use one CPU and sequential starts.

Use float64 throughout. Reject nonfinite parent values, line coefficients, roots, candidate vectors, and scores. Root discriminant tolerance, stable quadratic roots, bounded bisection inputs, and duplicate merging prevent avoidable numerical failures. Keep all trial vectors within the feasible pair interval; use the capped-simplex helper only as joint feasibility restoration. If a hull or line calculation fails, skip that pair. If a start fails, retain the validated global incumbent and fallbacks. The finite start, pair, sweep, bisection, and root loops define termination. This is a local search and must not be represented as a global certificate.

6. Runtime safeguards and return contract
The generated program must perform parent parsing, dimension selection, feasibility restoration, all exact score evaluations, search, and fallback selection when the harness later calls run(). Check the vector shape and finite values before scoring; require exact box bounds and both NumPy and stable mass errors no greater than 1e−10 before retaining any candidate. Implement the authoritative score as max(np.correlate(h,1−h,mode='full')*(2.0/n)); do not return a line-search polynomial value or any surrogate.

Initialize and score constant_h before entering search, and store a feasible parent-derived fallback whenever possible. A failed root calculation, projection, candidate check, or local search must leave a validated incumbent available. Keep the parent fallback even when another candidate becomes the incumbent. Revalidate the final vector, restore it only with the joint capped-simplex procedure, recompute its exact score, and fall back to the parent candidate or constant vector if any final operation fails. Return only the required three-tuple with n_points matching the vector length. The source must implement these operations; it must not claim that it ran, verified a bound, or reached the requested target.
